entries.label: Effect of entry cost on the entry rate of naturally high-entry industries
entries.units: percentage points of entry rate (high- minus low-natural-entry industry) per unit change in ln(entry cost ÷ income per head)

citation.authors: Leora Klapper, Luc Laeven and Raghuram Rajan
citation.title: Entry regulation as a barrier to entrepreneurship
citation.publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research, Working Paper 10380 (March 2004)
citation.locator: §4.1, p. 15 (PDF p. 16); log definition of EntCost, p. 14 (PDF p. 15); Table 7, column (i), p. 42 (PDF p. 43)

entries.quote: Following their work, we term the log of this variable EntCost. … The coefficient estimate suggests that the difference in entry rates between retail and pulp in the Czech Republic (which is at the 25th percentile in terms of EntCost with entry costs equal to 8% of per capita GNP) is 0.5 percentage points higher than the difference in entry rates between the same industries in Italy (which is at the 75th percentile in terms of EntCost with entry costs equal to 20% of per capita GNP).
entries.derivation: The paper's regressor is the log of entry cost. Moving from 20% to 8% of GNP per head is Δln = ln(8/20) = −0.916 and raises the retail-minus-pulp entry gap by 0.5 pp, so ε = 0.5 ÷ (−0.916) = −0.546 pp per log point (derived). Range: the Table 7 column (i) coefficient is −0.175 with standard error 0.047; its 95% interval (−0.267 to −0.083) scales ε to −0.833 and −0.258.
entries.notes: Retail is at the 75th and pulp and paper at the 25th percentile of US entry rates (the paper's proxy for natural entry), so ε is a difference between a high- and a low-natural-entry industry; the tool applies it only to naturally high-entry industries (A-P03). The traceability's earlier linear reading (0.5 pp per 12 pp of entry cost) is replaced by this log form (A-P11), which needs a baseline entry cost (entry c4.entry-cost-au.dj2002). The 2004 working paper was read; the 2006 Journal of Financial Economics version was not checked. Tobit estimates.

entries.label: Baseline cost of starting a simple firm in Australia

citation.authors: Simeon Djankov, Rafael La Porta, Florencio Lopez-de-Silanes and Andrei Shleifer
citation.title: The regulation of entry
citation.locator: Table III, Panel A, row 'Australia', column 'Cost', p. 18
citation.version: Copy of the journal article hosted at stanford.edu

entries.quote: The table also reports the time, direct cost (as a fraction of GDP per capita in 1999) associated with meeting government requirements … Australia 2 0 0 1 0 1 2 0.0225 0.0305 20,050
entries.derivation: Value = the Table III 'Cost' column for Australia (0.0225 of GDP per head) × 100. Fixed: a measured statistic.
entries.notes: Two procedures and two business days; 0.0305 when the entrepreneur's time is valued. Klapper, Laeven and Rajan use the same Djankov et al. measure, labelled as a share of per capita GNP. With the log form of F-C4-01 (A-P11) this is the baseline entry cost for every industry, which is a strong simplification: it is a 1999 measure for one simple start-up, not an industry's own entry cost. A user who knows an industry's entry cost should enter it.

entries.label: Extra speed of convergence to the global frontier per percentage point of industry entry rate
entries.units: change in convergence speed per percentage point of entry rate

citation.authors: Dan Andrews, Jonathan Hambur, David Hansell and Angus Wheeler
citation.title: Reaching for the stars: Australian firms and the global productivity frontier
citation.locator: Table 2, column (2) 'Entry', and its notes, p. 10 (PDF p. 13)

entries.quote: Entry rate x distance from frontier 0.009** (0.003) … The coefficients on the interaction terms estimate the additional convergence speed associated with a 1 percentage point increase in turnover, entry and exit rates.
entries.derivation: Value = the Table 2 column (2) coefficient (0.009). Range = its 95% interval from the reported standard error: 0.009 ± 1.96 × 0.003.
entries.notes: Grade C (owner decision, 23 Oct 2026; A-P17): a within-Australia panel correlation (industry-year fixed effects), not a causal policy elasticity, so economy-wide results resting on it are shown as indicative (plan §6.6). The paper publishes no sample mean of the distance to the frontier (variables are demeaned), so the gap in F-C4-03 has no default (A-P12). The text's illustration (8% to 16% entry raises convergence speed by 4.8 points) equals 0.006 × 8, the turnover coefficient, not 0.009 × 8 = 7.2; the library uses the Table 2 entry coefficient. Baseline convergence speed at the average entry rate: 0.415.

entries.label: Speed of convergence to the global frontier at the average entry rate (share of the log gap closed a year)
entries.units: share of the log distance from the frontier closed a year

citation.authors: Dan Andrews, Jonathan Hambur, David Hansell and Angus Wheeler
citation.title: Reaching for the stars: Australian firms and the global productivity frontier
citation.locator: Table 2, column (2) 'Distance from frontier', and its notes, p. 10 (PDF p. 13)

entries.quote: Distance from frontier 0.418*** 0.415*** 0.423*** (0.011) (0.012) (0.012) … For example, Column 2 implies that an industry with the average firm entry rate has an estimated convergence speed of 0.415.
entries.derivation: Value = the Table 2 column (2) coefficient on the distance from the frontier (0.415), which the notes read as the convergence speed at the average entry rate because the variables are demeaned. Range = its 95% interval from the reported standard error: 0.415 ± 1.96 × 0.012.
entries.notes: Grade C, as β₂ (A-P17): the same within-Australia panel regression. The dependent variable is firm labour productivity growth (value added per worker; the paper's section 3), so C4's productivity effect enters Layer B as labour productivity. A speed of 0.415 a year is fast and may include mean reversion in firm productivity; it sets how quickly C4's effect arrives (F-B-04) and the size of the long-run effect, gap × Δλ/(λ + Δλ) (A-P30).
